correctness.rationale: Homogeneity and forbidden triangles give exactly I^2 nonadjacent and D adjacent injective pair types. The integer sign test is exact. All 2^{n choose 2} labelled graphs for n<=5, every eligible missing-edge augmentation and every S5 relabelling of a decrease are exhausted by the supplied verifier. Direct full-graph extension enumeration independently matches three witnesses. Multiplication by (2,3) under an isolated vertex proves persistence. The six-point connected witness is checked directly.

originality.rationale: The normalized two-type edge-insertion reversal and sharp complete five-vertex marked classification were compared against the original Henson and Conant type theory, the published specialized multipartite Henson two-type calculation, an independent-set enumeration paper, and a five-site dynamic adsorption theorem. None states the same ratio, graph domain and sharp boundary. The exhaustive finite classification is specific and structurally distinct. Unindexed prior results remain possible; no independent priority certification is claimed.
residual_risks: A prior combinatorial study of normalized disjoint-independent-set partition functions may exist under a different name and contain the same five-vertex table.
General type-enumeration algorithms could be specialized to reproduce the result, but no examined source stated the sharp marked classification.
The independence-count paper was only checked at abstract level; it was not used as conclusive evidence of noncoverage.

value.rationale: A single added named adjacency can counterintuitively decrease the normalized proportion of *adjacent* fresh pair types. The sharp global onset at five, its complete two-orbit classification, the strictly later connected-base onset at six, and infinite persistence distinguish a natural boundary for finite-base type statistics. This is not a renaming of a known count or an unsupported sample: it measures the failure of a natural monotonicity heuristic in a homogeneous structure and completely classifies its first occurrence.
